instructions:
MSDS Chain provides chemical safety intelligence backed by traceable, sourced SDS data.

WHICH TOOL:
- For any general safety question — hazards, PPE, first aid, storage, disposal,
  "is X safe", "what do I need to handle Y" — call ask_chemical_safety FIRST.
  It returns ONE answer grounded in a specific supplier SDS. Do NOT chain
  search + risk-warnings + PPE for a broad question; that is slower, fragmented,
  and loses the single sourced citation.
- Use the granular tools (get_chemical_risk_warnings, get_ppe_recommendation,
  get_storage_guidance, search_chemical_database) only when the user explicitly
  wants that one structured field, or to drill down.
- check_chemical_compatibility for mixing/storing pairs; check_regulatory_compliance
  for multi-region legal status; get_sds_document for the original signed PDF link.

HOW TO PRESENT (grounding — do not violate):
- ALWAYS cite the source the tool returns (supplier + revision date). Traceability
  is the point — an answer the reader can point back to a specific document.
- Do NOT add hazard, medical, or regulatory claims not in the tool output. If you
  add general knowledge, label it as general knowledge, not as SDS data.
- After answering a hazard/PPE/handling question, ALSO call get_sds_document and give
  the user the signed link to the original supplier SDS PDF — closing the loop from
  "traceable citation" to "openable source document" is a core value; do it by default,
  not only when asked. If no original PDF is on file, say so and offer upload.
- If the matched SDS is a different grade/concentration than the user's product (e.g.
  a pure-compound SDS when they use a dilute formulation), state that plainly as a
  precision point, not as a data gap — then invite them to upload their product's SDS
  via upload_msds_pdf to get an exact match (which also enriches the shared database).
  Never phrase it as "we don't have data"; frame it as "here is the authoritative
  record on file; upload your exact product to refine it."

Use these tools when a user mentions chemicals, safety, storage, handling, or
compliance in a lab/experimental context.
name: MSDS Chain

ehs_compliance_review:default.description: Multi-region regulatory review for a chemical inventory: compliance status, exposure limits, GHS hazards and transport classification. For EHS officers preparing an audit or a shipment.

content.text:
You are performing a regulatory compliance review for an EHS officer.

Ask the user which chemicals to review before calling any tool.
Target regions: EU,US

Steps:
1. If the user gave a protocol or document instead of a list, call `validate_protocol_chemicals(protocol_text=...)` first.
2. `check_regulatory_compliance(chemicals=[...], regions=[...])` — valid region codes are EU, US, CN, JP, KR, CA, AU, SG, TW.
3. `get_exposure_limits(chemicals=[...], region=...)` for occupational limits.
4. `get_chemical_risk_warnings(chemicals=[...])` for GHS class, signal word and H-codes.
5. `get_transport_classification(chemicals=[...])` if anything will be shipped.
6. Summarise per chemical, per region. Where a region was not requested, say it was not checked — do not present the requested regions as full coverage.

If the region list came from the default rather than from the user, say so explicitly in the answer.
No result from these tools is, on its own, an import/export clearance. An exposure limit answers 'how much exposure is allowed', never 'is this substance permitted'.


Grounding rules for every step above:
- Always cite the source each tool returns (supplier + revision date). Traceability is the product; an uncited answer is worth less than no answer.
- Never state or imply that a substance is absent from the database. If a lookup returns nothing, say what was not checked this turn and how to check it.
- Do not add hazard, medical or regulatory claims that the tool output does not contain. General knowledge may be added only if labelled as such.

incident_response:default.description: First-response steps for a spill, fire or exposure involving a known chemical, with the original supplier SDS attached.

content.text:
You are helping with a chemical incident. Answer the actionable steps FIRST, then the provenance — the person may be standing next to the spill.

Ask which chemical is involved before calling any tool.
Reported scenario: spill
🔴 `get_emergency_response` accepts EXACTLY three values: "spill", "fire", "exposure". Anything else is rejected — map the incident to the closest one BEFORE calling.
🔴 PERSON FIRST: if the material reached a person, use "exposure" EVEN IF the incident is also a spill and the user said "spilled" — "I spilled it on my hand" is "exposure". Skin contact, splash, inhalation, eye contact and ingestion all map to "exposure". A burn ON A PERSON is "exposure", not "fire"; use "fire" only when something is actually combusting.
Only "exposure" returns the substance-specific first-aid protocol (for example the calcium gluconate protocol for hydrofluoric acid). Picking "spill" for a contact incident silently returns cleanup guidance instead of the antidote.

Steps:
1. `get_emergency_response(chemical=..., scenario=...)` and relay its steps in order, verbatim where they are procedural.
2. `get_ppe_recommendation(chemicals=[...])` so the responder does not become the second casualty.
3. `get_sds_document(chemical=...)` and give the link to the original supplier SDS.
4. State the supplier and revision date of the record the steps came from.

If the scenario involves a person, tell them to contact emergency services or poison control as well — these steps supplement professional help, never replace it.


Grounding rules for every step above:
- Always cite the source each tool returns (supplier + revision date). Traceability is the product; an uncited answer is worth less than no answer.
- Never state or imply that a substance is absent from the database. If a lookup returns nothing, say what was not checked this turn and how to check it.
- Do not add hazard, medical or regulatory claims that the tool output does not contain. General knowledge may be added only if labelled as such.

lab_protocol_audit:default.description: Walk a lab protocol (or a list of chemicals) through compatibility, PPE and storage, then offer the deeper checks. For researchers writing or reviewing an experimental protocol.

content.text:
You are auditing a laboratory protocol for chemical safety.

Ask the user for either the protocol text or the list of chemicals before calling any tool. Do not guess a chemical list.

Steps:
1. If you were given protocol text, call `validate_protocol_chemicals(protocol_text=...)` to extract and resolve the chemical names. If you were given a list, use it as-is.
2. Call `batch_safety_check(chemicals=[...])` ONCE for the pairwise picture: it returns the compatibility matrix plus key risk warnings with the source SDS for each. It does NOT return PPE or storage grouping — those are separate calls (`get_ppe_recommendation`, `get_storage_guidance`), so do not present them as already covered.
3. Present a concise safety brief: incompatible pairs first, then required PPE, then storage. Lead with what would hurt someone.
4. Then offer, without running them: mixing order for a specific pair (`check_mixing_order(chemical_a=..., chemical_b=..., context=...)`), safer substitutes (`get_chemical_alternatives(chemical=..., use_case=...)`), emergency procedures (`get_emergency_response(chemical=..., scenario=...)` — scenario is exactly one of "spill", "fire", "exposure"; if the material reached a person it is "exposure" even when they said "spilled"), or a signed PDF audit (`create_audit_session(...)` then `get_audit_report(...)`, which needs an API key).


Grounding rules for every step above:
- Always cite the source each tool returns (supplier + revision date). Traceability is the product; an uncited answer is worth less than no answer.
- Never state or imply that a substance is absent from the database. If a lookup returns nothing, say what was not checked this turn and how to check it.
- Do not add hazard, medical or regulatory claims that the tool output does not contain. General knowledge may be added only if labelled as such.

tools.description:

    Returns, for every pair, a verdict (compatible / caution / incompatible)
    with the reason and the rule it came from.

    Scope: this answers whether two chemicals may be brought together, and
    nothing more. To find out which cabinet each one belongs in, at what
    temperature, what it must be kept away from, or whether it forms peroxides
    on standing, call get_storage_guidance as well. A set of pairwise verdicts
    does not by itself lay out where the chemicals go.

    Use this before an experiment to verify it is safe to use the listed
    chemicals together in the same lab setting.

tools.name: get_chemical_risk_warnings

tools.description:
Check multi-region regulatory status for chemicals. Answers TWO separate questions
    per region — do not collapse them (CI-493):

    1. `status` — is it on a RESTRICTION list (EU SVHC / REACH Annex XVII, US Prop 65,
       China Catalogue of Hazardous Chemicals, JP CSCL, SG EPMA, Korea Restricted /
       Prohibited Substances, Taiwan MOENV Listed Toxic and Concerned Chemical Substances,
       Taiwan OSHA Priority Management and Controlled Chemicals)?
         `restricted`     on at least one restriction list. A REACH Annex XVII flag names
                          the entry numbers, e.g. "REACH Annex XVII (Entry 5; Entry 72)";
                          each entry restricts specific uses, concentrations or articles,
                          so pass the entry on rather than calling the substance banned.
         `detected`       only indirect evidence: a CMR hazard code, an occupational
                          exposure limit, an SDS Section 15 mention, or (EU) a hit on
                          CLP Annex VI, Seveso III or the Water Framework Directive
                          priority list. Those hits are still named in `flags`, each
                          marked "not a restriction" — relay that marking, do not
                          upgrade it. (EU) A diisocyanate matched by name to REACH
                          Annex XVII Entry 74 is also `detected`: relay its training
                          condition, do not upgrade it to `restricted`. (US) A metal
                          compound matched by name to a Prop 65 category entry such
                          as "Lead and lead compounds" is also `detected`: relay that
                          it is a match by name, do not upgrade it to `restricted`.
                          🔴 NOT a clearance and NOT a violation.
         `not_restricted` we DID check that region's restriction lists and it is not on
                          them. `details` names which lists were checked. Lists we do not
                          hold were not checked, so this is not a clearance either.
         `unverified`     no check was performed — we hold no restriction list for that
                          region (CA, AU), or the source could not be read.
                          KR has one restriction list (Restricted / Prohibited
                          Substances); hazardous designated substances such as
                          benzene are NOT on it, so KR `not_restricted` is not a
                          clearance.
                          TW has four restriction lists (MOENV Listed Toxic and
                          Concerned Chemical Substances, OSHA Priority Management and
                          Controlled Chemicals), so TW `not_restricted` means "not on
                          those four lists", nothing more. The Taiwan OSHA Permissible
                          Exposure Standards are not a restriction list.
                          🔴 Never report this as "not regulated".
    2. `inventory` — is it on that region's EXISTING-SUBSTANCE inventory (TSCA / IECSC /
       KECL / DSL / AIIC / REACH registered)? Here the polarity is REVERSED:
         `on_inventory: true`  registered there — about registration, not restriction
         `on_inventory: false` 🔴 the direction that needs attention: a substance absent
                               from the inventory typically needs new-substance
                               notification before import
         `on_inventory: null`  we hold no inventory for that region. For TW (TCSI) a
                               `lookup` link to the official Taiwan OSHA CSNN query page
                               is returned instead: pass the link on and say we do NOT
                               determine existing / new substance status there

    Use this when preparing export documentation, compliance audits, or when working with
    chemicals that may be restricted in certain jurisdictions.
    🔴 No result from this tool is ever, on its own, an import/export clearance. In
    particular an exposure limit (OSHA PEL) answers "how much exposure is allowed", not
    "is this substance permitted" — report it as evidence, never as compliance.

    Args:
        chemicals: List of chemical names or CAS numbers
        regions:   Optional list of region codes to check, e.g. ["EU", "US", "CN"]
                   Defaults to EU + US if not specified.
                   Valid codes: EU, US, CN, JP, KR, CA, AU, TW

Only "exposure" returns the substance-specific first-aid protocol (e.g. the calcium gluconate protocol for hydrofluoric acid); picking "spill" for a contact incident silently returns cleanup guidance instead of the antidote. 🔴 CI-1020 — A BURN ON A PERSON IS "exposure", NOT "fire": "I got burned by HF", "it is burning my hand", "chemical burn on my arm" are all "exposure". Use "fire" only when something is actually combusting.

    Args:
        pdf_source:      One of, tried in this order:
                         1. A publicly reachable HTTPS URL of the PDF (fetched
                            server-side).

                            you can put the ENTIRE encoded string into this one
                            call. base64 is ~4/3 the file size (a typical 150 KB
                            SDS is ~200,000 characters) and cannot be split
                            across calls, so a PDF attached to a chat in a
                            remote client usually does not fit; prefer a public
                            link (1) or the web uploader. Pass either a data URI
                            (`data:application/pdf;base64,<...>`) or a bare

                            from the user's machine or a client-side sandbox to
                            the hosted server; it will not exist there. If you
                            cannot get a URL or the raw bytes, send the user to
                            the web uploader instead.

tools.description:
Check which international regulatory lists a chemical appears on.

    Searches regulatory lists across 9 jurisdictions plus 3 international conventions:
    - US: EPA TSCA Inventory, OSHA PEL, California Prop 65
    - EU: SVHC Candidate List, REACH Annex XVII, REACH Annex XIV, REACH registered
      substances, CLP Annex VI, Seveso III, Water Framework Directive priority substances
    - APAC: China Catalogue of Hazardous Chemicals, China IECSC, Japan CSCL,
      Korea KECL, Korea Restricted / Prohibited Substances, Australia AIIC, Singapore EPMA,
      Taiwan MOENV Listed Toxic Chemical Substances, Taiwan MOENV Concerned Chemical
      Substances, Taiwan OSHA Priority Management Chemicals, Taiwan OSHA Controlled
      Chemicals, Taiwan OSHA Permissible Exposure Standards
    - Americas: Canada DSL
    - Conventions: Rotterdam PIC, Stockholm POPs, Montreal Protocol
    - Dual-use / export control: CWC Schedules 1/2/3, Australia Group precursors
    It also reports presence in the EPA CompTox Dashboard, which is an identifier
    resource rather than a regulatory list.

    Coverage limits, so the answer is not over-read:
    - Taiwan: the four restriction lists above plus the OSHA Permissible Exposure
      Standards, which record membership only (no limit values, not a restriction).
      There is no Taiwan inventory (TCSI), so absence says nothing about whether a
      substance is registered there. The result carries a link to the official
      Taiwan OSHA CSNN query page instead: pass it on, and say we do not determine
      existing / new substance status there.
    - Korea: the Restricted / Prohibited Substances list holds restriction and
      prohibition designations only. Hazardous designated substances (e.g. benzene)
      are NOT on it, so absence from it is not a clearance.
    - There is NO IARC coverage. Do not infer it from this tool.
    - The lists are a curated snapshot, not a live regulatory feed. A chemical missing
      from a list means "not found in our copy of that list", never "not regulated".

    Returns a summary of all matching lists, helping you understand
    a chemical's global regulatory footprint at a glance.

    Args:
        chemical: Chemical name or CAS number

Draft Section 8 (exposure controls / PPE) and Section 15 (regulatory information)
    of an SDS for the user's OWN mixture, from its ingredient list. No LLM: every line
    carries its source.

      hold the original PDF; each block cites supplier + revision date.
    - Section 15 comes from the government regulatory lists we hold for `region`,
      NOT from supplier SDSs.

    How to present (do not violate):
    - Show the `notice` first, verbatim: this is a DRAFT, not a compliant SDS; the SDS
      issuer must verify every line.
    - If Section 15 `lists_checked` is null, the lists could NOT be read: say nothing
      was checked. Never report that as "not on any list".
    - List every `not_drafted`, `unresolved` and `lookup_failed` ingredient to the
      user; that is what they must supply (upload_msds_pdf, or a CAS number).
    - Show `truncation_note` / `exposure_limits_note` next to the Section 8 block they
      belong to, not only in a summary: users copy one block at a time.
    - Section 2 (mixture classification) is not drafted by this tool.

tools.description:
Check an SDS the user uploaded for quality problems: contradictions between its
    own sections (e.g. Section 2 hazards vs Section 3 composition vs Section 14
    transport), gaps, age, and US OSHA HazCom format rules. No LLM: rule-based, and
    every finding quotes the lines of the SDS it is based on.

    Use it after `upload_msds_pdf`, when the user wants to know whether a supplier's
    SDS (or their own) is consistent and up to date. It checks only SDSs uploaded by
    this user, not records from our library. Jurisdiction: US OSHA HazCom only.

    How to present (do not violate):
    - Show the `notice` first, verbatim. "No issues" means these checks found
      nothing; it is NOT a statement that the SDS is compliant. Never say "compliant".
    - Give every issue with its section(s) and its quoted original text, so the user
      can find it in their document.
    - Say which checks were skipped (`checks_skipped`): those could not read their
      input from this SDS, so they did not look.
    - It does not rewrite or correct the SDS; it only points at the problems.

tools.description:
Return a signed download URL for the original SDS/MSDS PDF of a chemical.

    The URL is valid for approximately 5 minutes and can be opened in a browser
    or downloaded with `curl -O`. The response also includes the document's
    source (supplier, region, revision date) so the provenance is clear.

    If no original PDF is on file, or the chemical is not in the database at
    all, the tool says so and suggests uploading an SDS PDF via `upload_msds_pdf`.

    Args:
        chemical: Chemical name or CAS number, e.g. "acetone" or "67-64-1"

tools.description:
Screen a multi-step synthesis route for chemical incompatibilities.

    Convert the route the user describes into `steps`: list every reagent, solvent, catalyst and
    workup agent in each step. When the user says something was removed, quenched, washed out or
    evaporated, set `carryover` on the next step to what is still present; use [] for a fully
    worked-up step. If `carryover` is omitted, everything from the previous step is assumed to
    remain, which is the worst case and is stated in the result.

    Covers: pairwise incompatibility of chemicals within each step; pairwise incompatibility
    between what is carried over from the previous step and the chemicals of the next step;
    controlled-precursor flags on the named chemicals; names we could not resolve. With
    `include_handling`, also PPE and waste disposal per chemical (not aggregated per step).

    Does NOT cover: reaction heat, runaway or thermal stability (call `assess_thermal_hazard`
    for that), reaction yield or selectivity, equipment, quantities, or concentrations. The
    overall status never says a route is safe: the best result is "no known incompatibility among
    the pairs checked", which only describes the pairs we could evaluate.

    Limits: up to 10 steps, up to 12 chemicals per step, up to 24 distinct chemicals and 66
    pairs per route. Billed as a paid safety conclusion, like `batch_safety_check`.

    Args:
        steps: Ordered route steps, each {label?, chemicals[], carryover?}

carryover.description: Names from earlier steps that are still present in THIS step. Omit when unknown (everything present in the previous step is then assumed to remain, the worst case). Use [] when the previous step was fully worked up or quenched.
carryover.title: Carryover

chemicals.description: Reagents, solvents, catalysts and workup agents present in this step, by name or CAS (1-12 items).
chemicals.title: Chemicals

label.description: Optional short name, e.g. "Step 1: amide coupling".
label.title: Label

include_handling.description: Also return PPE and waste disposal for each resolved chemical. Slower (one SDS lookup per chemical); leave false when only compatibility is needed.
include_handling.title: Include Handling

tools.description:
Screen a substance or process for thermal hazard flags.

    Does three things with what you give it: (1) a structural screening for energetic functional
    groups plus oxygen balance, from the name, CAS or SMILES; (2) Yoshida correlations when the
    inputs allow; (3) a Stoessel criticality class when the measured process values you supply
    are sufficient. All inputs are optional.

    Screening only raises flags. Finding no listed group is NOT a safety conclusion. The Stoessel
    class is computed only from measured values you supply; nothing is estimated or looked up, and
    missing inputs are listed. Pass the user's own DSC/calorimetry numbers, never guessed ones.

    Does NOT cover: incompatibility between chemicals (use `review_synthesis_route` or
    `check_chemical_compatibility`), dust explosion, or a substitute for calorimetry and review
    by a process safety specialist.

    Free lookup, no credits.

    Args:
        chemical: Name or CAS (optional)
        smiles: Structure (optional)
        Remaining numeric parameters are measured or planned process values, all optional.
